title: The Field of Fractions and Localisation

items.title: Multiplicative subsets and the localisation $S^{-1}R$ as equivalence classes of fractions
The localisation relation is an equivalence relation and fraction arithmetic is well defined
items.strategy: For $(r,s)\sim(r',s')$ use a witness $u\in S$ with $u(rs'-r's)=0$. Prove reflexivity and symmetry directly and prove transitivity by multiplying the two witness equations by the missing denominators and witnesses. Then check that changing either representative preserves $(rs'+r's)/(ss')$ and $rr'/(ss')$, and verify the commutative-ring laws through representatives. Keep the zero-ring case: the construction allows $0\in S$.

items.title: Equality, vanishing, and the kernel of the localisation map
items.strategy: Unpack the defining relation to prove $r/s=r'/s'$ iff some $u\in S$ kills $rs'-r's$, and specialize to $r/s=0$. Deduce $\ker(R\to S^{-1}R)=\{r:\exists s\in S,\ sr=0\}$, that the map is injective exactly when every element of $S$ is a non-zero-divisor, and that $S^{-1}R$ is the zero ring exactly when $0\in S$. Separate the allowed zero-ring boundary explicitly.

items.title: Universal property of localisation: maps that invert $S$ factor uniquely through $S^{-1}R$
items.strategy: For a unital ring homomorphism $f:R\to A$ with every $f(s)$ a unit, define $\bar f(r/s)=f(r)f(s)^{-1}$. Use a witness for fraction equality to prove representative independence, then verify addition, multiplication, and identity. The factorisation through $r\mapsto r/1$ is immediate, and $r/s=(r/1)(s/1)^{-1}$ forces uniqueness. Include the $0\in S$ case: then such an $f$ can exist only when $A$ is the zero ring.

items.title: A localisation is unique up to a unique isomorphism compatible with the map from $R$
items.strategy: Apply the universal property in both directions to two $R$-algebras that invert $S$ and satisfy the factorisation property. Each composite is an endomorphism compatible with the structure map, so uniqueness makes both composites identities.

items.title: A fraction $r/s$ is a unit in $S^{-1}R$ exactly when $ar\in S$ for some $a\in R$
items.strategy: If $ar\in S$, exhibit $as/(ar)$ as an inverse. Conversely, if $r/s$ has inverse $b/t$, equality $rb/(st)=1$ supplies $u\in S$ with $u(rb-st)=0$, hence $(ub)r=ust\in S$. Check that the criterion correctly makes every $s/1$ a unit and treats the zero localisation without cancellation.

items.title: Principal localisation $R_f=\{1,f,f^2,\ldots\}^{-1}R$
Localising twice is localising once at the multiplicative set generated by both denominator sets
items.strategy: Let $S,T\subseteq R$ be multiplicative and let $U$ be the multiplicative set generated by $S\cup T$. Use the universal property to construct mutually inverse maps between $U^{-1}R$ and the localisation of $S^{-1}R$ at the image of $T$. Verify each composite by uniqueness rather than manipulating nested representatives; record the principal special case $(R_f)_g\cong R_{fg}$.

items.title: The field of fractions $\operatorname{Frac}(D)=(D\setminus\{0\})^{-1}D$ of an integral domain
$\operatorname{Frac}(D)$ is a field and $d\mapsto d/1$ embeds the integral domain $D$
items.strategy: The complement of zero is multiplicative because $D$ has no zero divisors. The kernel criterion makes the canonical map injective. A nonzero fraction $r/s$ has $r\ne0$ and inverse $s/r$; combine this with the localisation ring laws and the distinctness of $0/1$ and $1/1$ to verify the published field definition without silently cancelling in a general ring.

items.title: Every injective ring map from a domain into a field factors uniquely through its field of fractions
items.strategy: If $j:D\to K$ is injective and $s\ne0$, then $j(s)\ne0$ and is invertible in the field $K$. Apply the localisation universal property to obtain the unique map $\operatorname{Frac}(D)\to K$, explicitly $r/s\mapsto j(r)j(s)^{-1}$. Prove it is injective from the zero criterion and the injectivity of $j$.

items.title: Fields of fractions are uniquely isomorphic over their embedded domain
items.strategy: Apply the field-of-fractions universal property in both directions and use its uniqueness clause to make the composites identities. State compatibility with the two specified embeddings of $D$, not literal equality of the ambient fields.

items.title: For a field $F$, $F(t)=\operatorname{Frac}(F[t])$ is its rational function field; in particular $\mathbb R(t)=\operatorname{Frac}(\mathbb R[t])$
items.strategy: First prove directly that a field is an integral domain, then use that a polynomial ring over a domain is a domain and apply the field-of-fractions construction to $F[t]$. Define $F(t)$ by this equality and spell out that its elements are fractions $p(t)/q(t)$ with $q\ne0$, modulo cross multiplication. Specialize to the published real field for the stable consequence needed by the two existing ordered-field items; define no order on it.

items.title: A local ring is a nonzero commutative ring with a unique maximal ideal
A nonzero commutative ring is local exactly when its nonunits form an ideal, exactly when one of $x$ and $1-x$ is a unit for every $x$
items.strategy: If there is one maximal ideal, use maximal-ideal existence on the proper principal ideal of a nonunit to show that the maximal ideal is exactly the set of nonunits; its ideal closure yields the $x$ versus $1-x$ condition. Conversely, use that condition to prove the nonunits are closed under subtraction and absorption, hence form a proper ideal containing every proper ideal and therefore the unique maximal ideal. Keep the nonzero-ring hypothesis visible.

items.title: Localisation at a prime ideal: $R_{\mathfrak p}=(R\setminus\mathfrak p)^{-1}R$
$R_{\mathfrak p}$ is local with unique maximal ideal $\mathfrak pR_{\mathfrak p}$
items.strategy: Primality makes $R\setminus\mathfrak p$ multiplicative. Show membership of the numerator in $\mathfrak p$ is independent of a fraction representative, so the displayed fractions form a proper ideal. A fraction outside it has numerator outside $\mathfrak p$ and is a unit by the localisation unit criterion; therefore every proper ideal lies inside it, making it the unique maximal ideal.

items.title: A local ring $R$ is canonically isomorphic to $R_{\mathfrak m}$ at its maximal ideal
items.strategy: The unit characterization says every element outside the unique maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ is already a unit of $R$. The localisation universal property therefore gives $R_{\mathfrak m}\to R$ inverse to the canonical map; establish both composites by the uniqueness clauses.

items.title: A local ring has no idempotents other than $0$ and $1$
items.strategy: If $e^2=e$, then $e(1-e)=0$. The local-ring criterion makes either $e$ or $1-e$ a unit. Multiplying the zero product by the corresponding inverse gives respectively $e=1$ or $e=0$; the argument also shows why the zero ring was excluded from the local-ring convention.

items.title: Ideals of $S^{-1}R$ correspond to $S$-saturated ideals of $R$, and prime ideals correspond to primes disjoint from $S$
items.strategy: For an ideal $I\subseteq R$, define its extension $S^{-1}I=\{r/s:r\in I\}$ and verify representative independence. For an ideal $J\subseteq S^{-1}R$, contract along $R\to S^{-1}R$. Show every $J$ is the extension of its contraction because denominators are units, while contraction after extension is the saturation $\{r:\exists s\in S,\ sr\in I\}$. Restrict the bijection to prime ideals by checking properness is equivalent to disjointness from $S$ and proving primality in both directions.

items.title: Localisation commutes with quotient rings: $S^{-1}R/S^{-1}I\cong \bar S^{-1}(R/I)$
items.strategy: Send $r/s+S^{-1}I$ to $(r+I)/(s+I)$, where $\bar S$ is the image of $S$ in $R/I$. Construct the map first from the localisation universal property and factor it through the quotient universal property. Construct the inverse from $R\to S^{-1}R/S^{-1}I$ by the same two universal properties, and prove the composites are identities on the canonical generators. This is the ring-level exact quotient compatibility available before modules and exact sequences.

items.title: $R_{\mathfrak p}/\mathfrak pR_{\mathfrak p}\cong\operatorname{Frac}(R/\mathfrak p)$ is the residue field at $\mathfrak p$
items.strategy: Apply quotient compatibility with $S=R\setminus\mathfrak p$. The image of $S$ in the domain $R/\mathfrak p$ is exactly its nonzero set, so the right side is its field of fractions. Use the quotient-domain characterization of prime ideals, and identify the left quotient by the unique maximal ideal of $R_{\mathfrak p}$ as its residue field.

title: The Field of Fractions and Localisation — Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: $\operatorname{Frac}(\mathbb Z)$ is canonically isomorphic to $\mathbb Q$
items.strategy: Map $a/b$ to the published rational class represented by $(a,b)$. Compare the two cross-multiplication equivalence relations, verify arithmetic, and use the field-of-fractions universal property together with the integer embedding in $\mathbb Q$ to identify the map canonically rather than only abstractly.

items.title: $\mathbb Z[1/6]$ consists exactly of rationals $a/6^n$ and inverts precisely the primes $2$ and $3$
items.strategy: Use the principal localisation at $6$ and its canonical embedding into $\mathbb Q$. Reduce every denominator to a power of $6$, verify closure by common denominators, and use prime divisibility to show that a prime is a unit exactly when it is $2$ or $3$. Distinguish the ring from the whole fraction field by showing $1/5$ is absent.

items.title: $\mathbb Z_{(p)}$ consists of rationals with denominator not divisible by $p$, has maximal ideal $p\mathbb Z_{(p)}$, and residue field $\mathbb F_p$
items.strategy: For a prime $p$, use $\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z\cong\mathbb Z/p$ and fieldness to show $p\mathbb Z$ is prime. Identify the localisation fractions inside $\mathbb Q$, apply the prime-localisation theorem for its maximal ideal, and specialize the residue-field theorem; the fraction field of $\mathbb Z/p$ is itself because every nonzero denominator is already a unit.

items.title: $F[x]_{(x)}$ is the ring of rational functions defined at $0$, with maximal ideal generated by $x$ and residue field $F$
items.strategy: Evaluation at zero identifies $F[x]/(x)$ with $F$, so $(x)$ is maximal and prime. A denominator lies outside $(x)$ exactly when its constant term is nonzero, giving the claimed rational-function description. Apply the local and residue-field theorems, and identify the residue map with evaluation at zero.

items.title: If $0\in S$, localisation collapses: $S^{-1}R$ is the zero ring
items.strategy: Use the equality criterion with the denominator witness $0$ to show every $r/s$ equals $0/1$. Conversely connect this computation to the general zero-localisation criterion, explaining why the usual convention $0\notin S$ is optional but often imposed to exclude this collapse.

items.title: Outside a domain, the nonzero elements need not be multiplicative: $2\cdot3=0$ in $\mathbb Z/6$
items.strategy: In the published quotient ring $\mathbb Z/6$, verify that the classes of $2$ and $3$ are nonzero while their product is the zero class. Thus $R\setminus\{0\}$ is not even a permissible denominator set, isolating exactly where the domain hypothesis enters the fraction-field construction.

items.title: Localising at a zero divisor need not be injective: inverting $3$ in $\mathbb Z/6$ kills $2$
items.strategy: Take the multiplicative set $S=\{1,3\}$ in $\mathbb Z/6$. It does not contain zero, but $3\cdot2=0$, so the localisation kernel criterion gives $2/1=0$ although $2\ne0$ in the source. Also check $1/1\ne0$ because neither denominator in $S$ is zero, so the target has not collapsed entirely.

items.title: The total quotient ring of a nondomain need not be a field: $Q(\mathbb Z/6)\cong\mathbb Z/6$
items.strategy: Define the total quotient ring by inverting all non-zero-divisors. In $\mathbb Z/6$, show the non-zero-divisors are exactly the units $1$ and $5$, so the localisation universal property makes the canonical map an isomorphism. The surviving nonzero zero divisors show that this ring is not a field.

title: Splitting Fields and the Existence of Roots

items.title: Polynomials that split and splitting fields of a polynomial or a family of polynomials
Kronecker's one-root step: adjoining a root removes a linear factor and lowers the remaining degree
items.strategy: For a nonconstant $f\in F[x]$, use the published irreducible-factor quotient construction to obtain an extension $K/F$ and a root $\alpha$. Apply the factor theorem in $K[x]$ to write $f=(x-\alpha)g$ and use degree additivity to get $\deg g=\deg f-1$. Preserve multiplicities by retaining repeated linear factors rather than passing to distinct roots.

items.title: Every nonzero polynomial over a field has a splitting field
items.strategy: Use strong induction on degree. A nonzero constant already splits over $F$. For positive degree, apply the one-root step to obtain $K/F$ and $f=(x-\alpha)g$ with smaller-degree $g\in K[x]$; take a splitting field of $g$ over $K$. The resulting field splits $f$, and the field generated over $F$ by all roots of $f$ is the whole result because it contains $\alpha$, hence $K=F(\alpha)$ after choosing the root-extension step minimally, and then all roots of $g$. State the zero polynomial exclusion explicitly.

items.title: Every finite family of nonzero polynomials has a splitting field, obtained from their product
items.strategy: For a nonempty finite family, form its product, which is nonzero because $F[x]$ is a domain. A field splits the product exactly when it splits every factor, and the roots of the product are the union of their roots, so the generated-field minimality clauses agree. For the empty family, use the empty product $1$ and the convention that its splitting field is $F$.

items.title: Inside a common extension, the splitting field of $fg$ is the composite of the splitting fields of $f$ and $g$
items.strategy: Let $E$ and $L$ be the subfields generated by the roots of $f$ and $g$ in a common extension. Their composite $EL$ contains both root sets and hence splits $fg$. Conversely every field in the ambient extension that splits $fg$ contains both $E$ and $L$, so composite minimality makes it contain $EL$; this proves that $EL$ is exactly the splitting field.

items.title: A field isomorphism transports polynomials coefficientwise and carries roots, factorizations, and splitting to roots, factorizations, and splitting
items.strategy: Extend $\sigma:F\to F'$ coefficientwise to $F[x]\to F'[x]$. Directly verify evaluation compatibility $\sigma(f(\alpha))=\sigma(f)(\sigma(\alpha))$ when the isomorphism is extended to ambient fields. Apply this to each linear factor, including repetitions, and use inverse transport for the converses.

items.title: A base-field isomorphism extends across simple adjunctions of corresponding roots of an irreducible polynomial
items.strategy: Let $\sigma:F\to F'$ and let $p\in F[x]$ be monic irreducible, with roots $\alpha$ of $p$ and $\beta$ of $\sigma(p)$. Use the two minimal-polynomial quotient descriptions to send the class of $g$ to the class of $\sigma(g)$. Prove representative independence, field-homomorphicity, bijectivity via $\sigma^{-1}$, and uniqueness from generation by the distinguished root.

items.title: A base-field isomorphism extends to an isomorphism between splitting fields of corresponding polynomials
items.strategy: Induct on the degree of the polynomial. Transport the polynomial along the base isomorphism, choose corresponding roots, and extend the base map across their simple adjunctions by the preceding lemma. Divide off the matched linear factors and apply the induction hypothesis to their splitting fields over the enlarged bases. Track the generated-field clauses so the terminal map has exactly the two given splitting fields as domain and codomain; include constants as the base case.

items.title: Any two splitting fields of a polynomial are isomorphic over the base field
items.strategy: Apply the isomorphism-extension theorem to the identity map of $F$ and the two splitting fields of the same polynomial. State only existence of an $F$-isomorphism: it is generally not unique, because roots may be permuted.

items.title: A degree-$n$ polynomial has a splitting field spanned over $F$ by at most $n!$ explicit root monomials
items.strategy: Follow the existence construction, adjoining roots $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_r$ while residual degrees strictly fall. At stage $i$, the minimal polynomial of $\alpha_i$ over the current field divides the residual polynomial, so its degree $d_i$ is at most the current residual degree. Repeatedly apply the published simple power-coordinate theorem to flatten every element into an $F$-linear combination of monomials $\alpha_1^{e_1}\cdots\alpha_r^{e_r}$ with $0\le e_i<d_i$. Their number is $\prod d_i\le n!$. Do not call this number $[E:F]$: general dimension and the tower law remain outside this page's prerequisites.

items.title: After adjoining one nonzero root $\alpha$ of $x^n-a$, all roots are $\zeta\alpha$ with $\zeta^n=1$
items.strategy: Assume $n\ge1$ and $a\ne0$. If $\beta^n=a=\alpha^n$, then $\zeta=\beta/\alpha$ satisfies $\zeta^n=1$, and conversely every such $\zeta$ makes $\zeta\alpha$ a root. Therefore the splitting field is generated by one root together with all $n$th roots of unity. Treat $a=0$ separately: $x^n$ has only the root $0$ and already splits over $F$.

items.title: Every $F$-endomorphism of a splitting field permutes the distinct roots and is an automorphism
items.strategy: Coefficientwise evaluation compatibility sends each root of $f$ to another root. A field homomorphism is injective, so on the finite set of distinct roots the induced self-map is a permutation. Since the splitting field is generated by those roots over $F$, its image contains every generator and is therefore the whole field; hence the endomorphism is an automorphism.

items.title: A normal algebraic extension is one in which every minimal polynomial with a root in the extension splits there
If $K/F$ is normal and $F\subseteq E\subseteq K$, then $K/E$ is normal
items.strategy: Let $\alpha\in K$. Its minimal polynomial $p_F$ over $F$ also shows that $\alpha$ is algebraic over $E$, and the minimal polynomial $p_E$ over $E$ divides $p_F$ in $E[x]$. Normality over $F$ makes $p_F$ split in $K[x]$; unique factorisation in $K[x]$ then makes its divisor $p_E$ split there as well. Since this holds for every $\alpha\in K$, the defining criterion gives normality over $E$.

items.title: A nonempty intersection of normal subextensions inside a common algebraic extension is normal
items.strategy: Let $M/F$ be algebraic and let $M/E_i/F$ be normal subextensions for $i$ in a nonempty index set. Their intersection $E$ is algebraic over $F$. For $\alpha\in E$, its minimal polynomial $p$ over $F$ splits in every $E_i$. Fix one index and factor $p$ there; comparison in the UFD $M[x]$ with the complete factorisation over any other $E_i$ shows that every root in the first factorisation lies in every $E_i$. Thus all roots lie in $E$, so $p$ splits in $E$. The nonempty hypothesis is explicit because an empty intersection would be the ambient field, which need not be normal.

items.title: An algebraic extension that is a splitting field of a polynomial is normal
items.strategy: Let $E/F$ be algebraic and the splitting field of $f$. For an irreducible $p\in F[x]$ with a root $\alpha\in E$, take a splitting field $\Omega/E$ of $p$ and a root $\beta\in\Omega$. The isomorphism $F(\alpha)\to F(\beta)$ extends to an isomorphism $E\to E(\beta)$ between the two splitting fields of $f$ over those simple extensions. Because $f$ already splits in $E$, every root of $f$ in $E(\beta)$ lies in $E$; the extended map therefore has image inside $E$, so $\beta$ lies in $E$. Thus every root of $p$ lies in $E$, and $p$ splits there. Keep algebraicity as an explicit hypothesis rather than importing its later transitivity proof.

items.title: An algebraic extension generated by elements whose minimal polynomials split in it is normal
items.strategy: Let $E=F(S)$ be algebraic, with the minimal polynomial over $F$ of every member of $S$ splitting in $E$. First prove the finite-support fact directly: the union of the fields $F(T)$ over finite $T\subseteq S$ is a subfield containing $F\cup S$, so generated-field minimality makes it all of $E$. Given $\beta\in E$, choose finite $T$ with $\beta\in F(T)$. If $T$ is empty then $\beta\in F$ and its minimal polynomial is linear. Otherwise collect in $E$ all roots of the minimal polynomials of the elements of $T$ and let $K$ be the subfield they generate. Then $K$ is the splitting field of their finite product, $K/F$ is algebraic because $K\subseteq E$, and the algebraic-splitting-extension proposition makes $K/F$ normal. Since $\beta\in K$, its minimal polynomial splits in $K$ and hence in $E$.

items.title: A normal extension generated by finitely many elements is the splitting field of the product of their minimal polynomials
items.strategy: Let $E=F(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_r)$ be normal. Each minimal polynomial $m_{\alpha_i}$ splits over $E$ by normality, so their product does. The field generated by all roots of that product is contained in $E$ and contains every chosen generator $\alpha_i$, hence equals $E$. For the empty generating family, record that $E=F$ is the splitting field of the constant polynomial $1$.

title: Splitting Fields and the Existence of Roots — Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: The base field is the splitting field of the empty family and of every nonzero constant polynomial
items.strategy: Use the empty union of root sets and the generated-subfield convention $F(\varnothing)=F$. A nonzero constant is already a scalar times the empty product of linear factors, so it has the same splitting field. Contrast this with the excluded zero polynomial, whose root set is every element of every extension and whose degree is undefined in the library.

items.title: The splitting field of $x^2-2$ over $\mathbb Q$ is $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)$, with roots $\pm\sqrt2$
items.strategy: Use Eisenstein at $2$ for irreducibility and the published nonnegative real square root to realize one root. Factor $(x-\sqrt2)(x+\sqrt2)$ and show that adjoining either root gives the same generated field. The simple power-coordinate theorem supplies the form $a+b\sqrt2$ without invoking general vector-space dimension.

items.title: The splitting field of $x^3-2$ over $\mathbb Q$ is $\mathbb Q(\sqrt[3]{2},\omega)$ with $\omega=(-1+i\sqrt3)/2$
items.strategy: Let $\alpha=\sqrt[3]{2}>0$ and verify $\omega^2+\omega+1=0$ and $\omega^3=1$ in $\mathbb C$. The three roots are $\alpha,\omega\alpha,\omega^2\alpha$, so their generated field is $\mathbb Q(\alpha,\omega)$. Eisenstein at $2$ makes $x^3-2$ irreducible, while the factorial-coordinate theorem gives an explicit spanning family of at most six monomials; do not assert a general tower-law degree calculation.

items.title: The splitting field of $x^4+2x^2-8$ over $\mathbb Q$ is $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2,i)$
items.strategy: Factor $x^4+2x^2-8=(x^2-2)(x^2+4)$ over $\mathbb Q$. Its roots in $\mathbb C$ are $\pm\sqrt2$ and $\pm2i$, so the field generated by all roots is exactly $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2,i)$. Check both containments from the displayed roots and generators.

items.title: The splitting field of $\{x^2-2,x^2-3\}$ over $\mathbb Q$ is $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2,\sqrt3)$
items.strategy: List the four roots and apply the finite-family definition. Prove the generated field equals the composite of the two quadratic splitting fields and also the splitting field of $(x^2-2)(x^2-3)$. Exhibit the spanning family $1,\sqrt2,\sqrt3,\sqrt6$ by reducing powers, without claiming linear independence or degree four.

items.title: Over $\mathbb F_2$, $x^4+x^2+1=(x^2+x+1)^2$ has two distinct roots, each repeated, in its four-element splitting field
items.strategy: Use the published field $\mathbb Z/2$ and check that $x^2+x+1$ has no root there, hence is irreducible. Form $K=\mathbb F_2[u]/(u^2+u+1)$; the second root is $u+1$, and characteristic two gives $(x^2+x+1)^2=x^4+x^2+1$. Thus $K$ is the splitting field while multiplicity remains visible.

items.title: Adjoining one root need not split the polynomial: $\mathbb Q(\sqrt[3]{2})$ does not split $x^3-2$
items.strategy: The field $\mathbb Q(\sqrt[3]{2})$ lies inside $\mathbb R$, while the other two roots $\omega\sqrt[3]{2}$ and $\omega^2\sqrt[3]{2}$ from the preceding example are nonreal. Therefore the real root field contains one root but not all roots, and is strictly smaller than the splitting field.

items.title: FALSE: the isomorphism between two splitting fields that fixes the base field is unique
items.strategy: Use the splitting field $E=\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)$ of $x^2-2$ twice. Both the identity and the map fixing $\mathbb Q$ and sending $\sqrt2$ to $-\sqrt2$ are field automorphisms, and they are distinct. This leaves the actual uniqueness theorem intact: the field is unique up to existence of an $F$-isomorphism, not up to a unique one.
